subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which two substances are the raw materials (reactants) of photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water to produce glucose and oxygen.

questions.q: Which pigment, found in chloroplasts, absorbs the light energy used in photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Chlorophyll in the chloroplasts absorbs light energy to drive photosynthesis.

questions.q: In terms of energy, photosynthesis is best described as a reaction that is:
questions.explain: Photosynthesis is endothermic because it absorbs (takes in) light energy from the surroundings.

questions.q: Which balanced symbol equation correctly represents photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Six molecules of carbon dioxide and water form one glucose molecule and six oxygen molecules.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a limiting factor of the rate of photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature can all limit the rate, whereas oxygen is a product, not a limiting factor.

questions.q: A plant is photosynthesising in a brightly lit room at 20°C. Increasing the light intensity further has no effect on the rate. Which factor is most likely limiting the rate?
questions.explain: When more light gives no further increase, another factor such as carbon dioxide concentration (or temperature) must be limiting the rate.

questions.q: What does the xylem tissue transport in a plant?
options: Sucrose from the leaves to the roots
Water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves
Oxygen from the leaves to the roots
Amino acids from the roots to the shoots
questions.explain: Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral ions upwards from the roots to the rest of the plant.

questions.q: What does the phloem tissue mainly transport?
questions.explain: Phloem transports dissolved sugars (mainly sucrose) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

questions.q: Why are mature xylem vessels well adapted to transport water?
options: They are living cells packed with cytoplasm
They are hollow, dead cells strengthened with lignin
They contain chloroplasts to make sugars
They have many mitochondria for active transport
questions.explain: Xylem vessels are dead, hollow tubes strengthened with lignin, allowing a continuous, unobstructed flow of water.

questions.q: The movement of dissolved sugars through the phloem is known as:
questions.explain: Translocation is the transport of dissolved sugars through the phloem, which can move in both directions.

questions.q: A ring of bark (containing phloem) is removed all the way around a tree trunk. Sugar builds up above the ring but the roots below eventually starve. This best demonstrates that:
options: Phloem carries sugars from leaves towards the roots
Water only moves upwards in phloem
Mineral ions are made in the leaves
questions.explain: Removing the phloem blocks translocation of sugars to the roots, so sugar accumulates above the cut and the roots starve.

questions.q: Transpiration is best defined as the:
options: Uptake of mineral ions by root hair cells
Loss of water vapour from the leaves and stems of a plant
Movement of sugars through the phloem
Absorption of carbon dioxide by the stomata
questions.explain: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant's surfaces, mainly through the stomata in the leaves.

questions.q: Which structures control the opening and closing of the stomata?
questions.explain: A pair of guard cells surrounds each stoma and controls whether it is open or closed.

questions.q: Which change in conditions would increase the rate of transpiration?
questions.explain: Wind removes water vapour from around the leaf, maintaining a steep concentration gradient and increasing transpiration.

questions.q: A potometer is a piece of apparatus used to measure the:
options: Rate of water uptake by a plant shoot
Mass of minerals absorbed by roots
questions.explain: A potometer measures the rate of water uptake by a cut shoot, which is used as an estimate of the transpiration rate.

questions.q: In a potometer experiment, a student uses a fan to blow air across the leaves. Compared with still air, the air bubble in the potometer will:
options: Move more slowly, showing reduced water uptake
Move more quickly, showing increased water uptake
questions.explain: Increased air movement raises the transpiration rate, so water is taken up faster and the bubble moves more quickly.

questions.q: Which plant hormone controls phototropism and gravitropism in shoots?
questions.explain: Auxin is the plant hormone that coordinates growth responses such as phototropism and gravitropism.

questions.q: A plant shoot growing towards a source of light is showing:
questions.explain: Growth towards light is positive phototropism, which helps the shoot maximise light for photosynthesis.

questions.q: How does auxin cause a shoot to bend towards light coming from one side?
options: Auxin builds up on the shaded side, making those cells elongate more so the shoot bends towards the light
Auxin builds up on the lit side, making those cells elongate more so the shoot bends away
Auxin destroys cells on the shaded side so the shoot shrinks towards the light
Auxin prevents all cell growth so the shoot stays straight
questions.explain: Auxin accumulates on the shaded side and promotes cell elongation there, so that side grows faster and the shoot bends towards the light.

questions.q: A gardener dips the cut ends of stem cuttings into rooting powder to help them grow roots. Which plant hormone is the active ingredient?
questions.explain: Auxins are used commercially in rooting powders to stimulate the growth of roots on stem cuttings.
